governanceNotes: D1 batch 51 (2026-09-24): one bounded association edge authored - knee disarticulation to phantom-limb-pain (rank 1) - classified ASSOCIATION_ONLY with etiologicalConsensus NOT_ESTABLISHED, vaNexusProbabilityAlignment NOT_ASSERTED, and hypothesizedOnly:true; mechanismCategory NEUROLOGICAL_DEGENERATION. The proposition rests on the Nees 2024 Heidelberg Amputation Registry cross-sectional study of 459 patients with lower-limb amputation (hip disarticulations 3.7% and knee disarticulations 3.5% of the cohort, transtibial 43% and transfemoral 39%, mean 15 years since amputation), in which 85% reported abnormal sensations and the prevalence of phantom limb pain, phantom limb sensation, and residual limb pain was 58%, 66%, and 46% respectively, and in which the occurrence of sensory disturbances other than residual limb pain was significantly affected by the level of amputation with age at amputation an independent risk factor; it rests also on the Kelle 2017 cross-sectional study of 101 lower-limb amputees stratified by amputation level, which found statistically significant differences in stump-pain and phantom-limb-pain intensity between levels with the most proximal group - hip disarticulation through knee disarticulation, including knee disarticulation - showing the highest early-postoperative visual-analogue scores, although that difference did not persist at six months. The level-stratified evidence places knee disarticulation in the proximal group with the highest early phantom-pain intensity.

Counter-evidence and caveat screens recorded 2026-09-24: (i) temporal attenuation - the Kelle cohort's higher proximal-group pain scores were present in the early postoperative period and had disappeared by the six-month assessment, so the edge does not assert a persistent level effect; (ii) cross-sectional design - the Heidelberg registry reports prevalence by level without an inception cohort or untreated comparison, so no incidence or individual probability can be inferred; (iii) multifactorial pain - the registry also reports residual limb pain in 46% and phantom sensation in 66%, and age at amputation was an independent risk factor, so level is one contributor among several; (iv) cause and comorbidity confounding - the registry's leading causes were trauma (32%) and neoplasm (22%) with peripheral artery disease and diabetes contributing, and these causes independently influence pain and stump outcomes.

Negative screens recorded 2026-09-24: (i) no knee-disarticulation-to-depressive-disorder edge - the amputation-or-loss-of-use container owns the generic post-amputation mood window (container guard); (ii) no contractures edge - the located knee-disarticulation literature quantifies reamputation (36% after knee disarticulation versus 15% after transfemoral reamputation), reoperation, prosthetic fitting, and mortality rather than stump contracture, and the knee-disarticulation stump preserves the femoral condyles as an end-bearing surface (zero-record and anatomy guards); (iii) no muscle-atrophy edge (zero-record guard); (iv) no loss-of-use-of-extremities edge - that identity is a rating-framework container for loss of use of a limb (rating-container guard); (v) no osteomyelitis or cellulitis edge - no condition-specific knee-disarticulation quantification of stump infection was retrieved in this batch window (zero-record guard); (vi) duplicate-scope note: the phantom-limb-pain identity's eight existing amputation-level windows are not pre-empted, and this batch adds the knee-disarticulation level to the same level-stratified evidence base.

nexusClaim.associationBasis: The Nees 2024 Heidelberg Amputation Registry cross-sectional study analysed 459 patients with lower-limb amputation (transfemoral 39%, transtibial 43%, partial foot 10%, hip disarticulation 3.7%, knee disarticulation 3.5%, hemipelvectomy 1%; mean 15 years since amputation) and found that 85% reported abnormal sensations, with prevalences of phantom limb pain of 58%, phantom limb sensation of 66%, and residual limb pain of 46%, that the occurrence of sensory disturbances with the exception of residual limb pain was significantly affected by the level of amputation, and that age at amputation was an independent risk factor for abnormal sensations; the Kelle 2017 cross-sectional study of 101 lower-limb amputees stratified by level found statistically significant between-group differences in stump-pain and phantom-limb-pain intensity in the early postoperative period, with the most proximal group - hip disarticulation through knee disarticulation, including knee disarticulation - showing the highest visual-analogue scores, a difference that did not persist at the six-month assessment; the literature documents a level-stratified phantom-pain burden that includes knee disarticulation without establishing that the amputation caused an individual's phantom pain.
nexusClaim.causationStatus: The mapping does not assert that knee disarticulation caused an individual's phantom limb pain: no inception cohort quantifies phantom-pain incidence after this amputation level, the located proximal-group elevation was an early-postoperative finding that had disappeared by six months, the registry is cross-sectional and reports phantom sensation and residual limb pain alongside phantom limb pain at comparable prevalences, age at amputation is an independent risk factor, and pre-amputation pain, residual-limb and stump pathology, neuroma, prosthetic-fit problems, radiculopathy, and complex regional pain syndrome independently produce limb pain after amputation - so no directional claim is made.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: A hypothesized deafferentation route is described for this amputation level: transection of the sciatic and femoral nerve supply at or above the knee removes peripheral input and triggers maladaptive cortical and spinal reorganization with ectopic firing at the stump neuroma and up-regulated dorsal-horn excitability, producing the phantom sensations that the level-stratified literature reports most intensely in the most proximal amputation group during the early postoperative period; the same mechanisms operate at every amputation level, so the level gradient is a severity modifier rather than a distinct mechanism and the individual course remains a hypothesis.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: This relationship is supported as an association only. Level-stratified amputation cohorts document phantom limb pain, phantom sensation, and residual limb pain at high prevalence including at knee disarticulation, but individual determination requires amputation documentation with level and date, a characterisation of the phantom experience with chronology and distribution, assessment of the residual limb and prosthesis, and exclusion of competing causes, with review by a qualified medical professional.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: Operative and amputation documentation (date, level, indication, whether the procedure was a primary amputation or a reamputation after a failed more distal amputation, wound healing, and stump findings); characterisation of the phantom experience with onset, frequency, duration, intensity, provoking and relieving factors, laterality, and its relationship to the missing segment, distinguished from phantom sensation, residual limb pain, and stump pain; assessment of the residual limb and prosthesis including socket fit, end-bearing tolerance, skin integrity, and gait; examination and, where indicated, imaging or electrodiagnostic evaluation for neuroma, heterotopic ossification, radiculopathy, or nerve entrapment; documentation of pre-amputation pain and of the cause of amputation (trauma, neoplasm, peripheral vascular disease, diabetes, or infection); exclusion of complex regional pain syndrome, referred spinal pain, and prosthetic-fit pain as competing causes; qualified clinical assessment of whether the amputation level materially contributed to the phantom pain
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: Residual limb pain, stump pain, or prosthetic-fit pain rather than phantom limb pain
Neuroma, heterotopic ossification, or nerve entrapment at the amputation site
Pre-amputation pain from the condition that led to amputation (including diabetic or vascular ischaemic pain)
Lumbar radiculopathy, spinal stenosis, or referred spinal pain
Complex regional pain syndrome of the residual limb

suggestions.rationale: Authored at ASSOCIATION_ONLY: a 459-patient amputation registry reported phantom limb pain in 58% and phantom sensation in 66% with level-dependent sensory disturbances, and a 101-patient level-stratified series reported the highest early postoperative phantom-pain intensity in the most proximal group that includes knee disarticulation. Because the registry is cross-sectional, the level gradient attenuated by six months, and multiple competing causes of post-amputation limb pain exist, the conservative standard keeps the edge at association only, consistent with the amputation-of-arm, amputation-of-foot, amputation-of-hand, amputation-of-leg, ankle-disarticulation, elbow-disarticulation, hip-disarticulation, and hemipelvectomy windows already carried by the phantom-limb-pain identity.
